outcome: Claimed false since 26 January 2024: James Freitag and Scott Mutchnik posted arXiv:2609.00436 on 31 August 2026 (one version as of my last check, 13 October 2026; not peer reviewed), constructing a supersimple theory in which forking is not witnessed by stable formulas, and crediting ChatGPT 5.6 / GPT-5.6 Sol with the construction; I found no independent verification reported in any source I could reach. Partial results on restricted cases (finite-rank supersimple reduction, countably categorical equivalence) and on an NSOP1 analogue also appeared in 2024 to 2026.
problem_asks: Single universal claim, as the Wikipedia bullet words it: for every simple first-order theory T, forking is witnessed by stable formulas. Unpacked: (1) the claim ranges over all simple theories, with no restriction to finite rank, supersimplicity, countable language, or omega-categoricity; (2) for each such T, for every type p over a set and every subset C over which p forks, some formula phi(x, b) in p (with b from the base) forks over C; (3) that phi(x, y), with parameters left as variables, is stable (has no order property). The bullet names no formulation. The literature gives several (over the empty set or over bases, strong and weak versions, global variants), and Freitag and Mutchnik state the Hart-Kim-Pillay formulation as their Conjecture 1.2: if a is not independent from b over C, some formula in tp(a/Cb) forks over C and its parameter-free version is stable. The record below uses that formulation as the reading of the bullet; which formulation the bullet means is not settled by the wording.

events.what_happened: Assaf Peretz, 'Geometry of forking in simple theories' (arXiv math/0412356, single version). Studies forking for U-rank 2 elements in supersimple omega-categorical theories, proves stable forking for such elements, and extends the analysis to U-rank 3 elements. Published in the Journal of Symbolic Logic, 71(1) 2006, pp. 347-359 (per search snippets; not opened).
events.revisions: v1 only on arXiv (18 Dec 2004). JSL publication 2006 from search snippets, not verified.
events.delivers: Stable forking for U-rank (SU-rank) 2 types in supersimple omega-categorical theories, plus structural results for rank 3. Restricted to omega-categorical supersimple theories of rank at most 2 (and the rank-3 analysis as the abstract describes it).
events.remains: Stable forking for general simple theories, non-omega-categorical theories, and higher rank. Mutchnik (2026) says Peretz's rank-3 universal result does not extend as stated to higher ranks.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record in model theory; refereed
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (2006, vol. 71 no. 1), per search snippets; refereeing not examined

events.direction: Positive: stable forking holds for the restricted class.

events.what_happened: Pourmahdian, 'The stable forking conjecture and generic structures', Archive for Mathematical Logic 42 (2003), 415-421, DOI 10.1007/s00153-002-0147-x. Abstract (via search snippet; paper not opened): for a simple theory built by the Fraisse-Hrushovski method, if forking coincides with d-independence, then the stable forking property holds. An undated report by D. M. Evans (imperial.ac.uk) says Evans and Pourmahdian had verified the conjecture for some Hrushovski-construction simple theories, and that Pourmahdian pursued a possible counterexample from predimensions; I could not read the outcome.
events.delivers: Stable forking for simple theories from the Fraisse-Hrushovski construction in which forking equals d-independence. Restricted class defined by a hypothesis (forking = d-independence).
events.remains: Simple theories outside that class, including those the paper does not cover; the Evans report's counterexample attempt is undetermined in what I could read.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (2003), per search snippet; refereeing not examined

events.what_happened: Byunghan Kim, 'Simplicity, and stability in there', Journal of Symbolic Logic 66(2) (2001), 822-836, DOI 10.2307/2695047. Abstract (via the Cambridge page): proves simplicity equivalent to symmetry of forking; for a one-based theory with elimination of hyperimaginaries, the stable formulas witness forking, so the stable forking property holds for such a theory.
events.delivers: Stable forking for one-based simple theories with elimination of hyperimaginaries. Restricted to one-based theories with EHI.
events.remains: Simple theories that are not one-based, or lack elimination of hyperimaginaries.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record in model theory; refereed
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (2001), per the Cambridge listing

events.what_happened: Byunghan Kim and Anand Pillay, 'Around stable forking', Fundamenta Mathematicae 170 (2001), 107-118, DOI 10.4064/fm170-1-6. Abstract (via the IMPAN page): discusses conjectures about when stable formulas account for forking in simple theories; if a simple theory has strong stable forking, every complete type is a nonforking extension of a type axiomatized by instances of stable formulas; gives a second treatment of Kim's canonical-bases result. Mutchnik (arXiv 2607.09069 v3, footnote 4) states 'the strong stable forking conjecture is known to be false in general', citing Kim and Pillay (2001). I did not confirm that statement in the 2001 text.
events.delivers: A conditional structure result for the strong variant of the conjecture (strong stable forking). Not the bullet's formulation as I read it.
events.remains: Whether the weak formulation holds in general; whether the strong variant is false in general, per the 2026 footnote (unverified here).

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (2001), per the IMPAN listing

events.doubts: The 2026 footnote's claim that the strong version is known false in general rests on a citation to this paper; I did not check whether the 2001 paper contains that result.
events.direction: Conditional structure result for the strong variant; the 2026 footnote reports the strong variant is false in general.

events.what_happened: Daniel Palacin and Frank Olaf Wagner, 'Elimination of Hyperimaginaries and Stable Independence in simple CM-trivial theories' (arXiv 1006.5526, v1 29 Jun 2010; v5 19 Mar 2012). Abstract: in a supersimple CM-trivial theory the independence relation is stable; such a theory eliminates hyperimaginaries whenever it eliminates finitary ones. Published Notre Dame J. Formal Logic 54 (2013), 541-551. Mutchnik (2026) attributes a countably-categorical equivalence to Corollary 4.4 of this paper.
events.delivers: Stability of the independence relation for supersimple CM-trivial theories. The abstract does not use the phrase 'stable forking'; that the result bears on the stable forking conjecture is my reading via Mutchnik (2026), not checked in the paper.
events.remains: Simple theories outside the CM-trivial class.

checked_by.who: Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic (refereed journal)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (2013), per arXiv journal reference

events.direction: Positive for a restricted class, if the stable-independence result is the stable forking property; this link is not established from the abstract.

events.what_happened: Daniel Palacin, 'On omega-categorical simple theories' (arXiv 1102.3631, v1 17 Feb 2011; v2 3 Nov 2011). Proves that countable omega-categorical simple CM-trivial theories are low, and that countable omega-categorical simple theories with strong stable forking are low; observes that simple theories of bounded finite weight are low.
events.delivers: Lowness for omega-categorical simple theories with strong stable forking, a variant of the bullet's property. Lowness is not the bullet's question.
events.remains: The weak formulation for omega-categorical simple theories; the strong variant is what is addressed.
events.direction: Positive for a variant (strong stable forking), restricted class; not the bullet's formulation.

events.what_happened: Enrique Casanovas and Joris Potier, 'Stable forking and imaginaries' (arXiv 1508.02199, v1 10 Aug 2015). Abstract: a theory T has stable forking if and only if T^eq has stable forking. Published Notre Dame J. Formal Logic 59(4) (2018), 497-502 (per search snippet).
events.delivers: An equivalence between stable forking for T and for T^eq, for an arbitrary theory T. It reduces the property to imaginaries and settles no instance of the conjecture by itself.
events.remains: Whether stable forking holds for any simple theory; the equivalence transfers the question, it does not answer it.

checked_by.who: Notre Dame Journal of Formal Logic (refereed journal)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (2018), per search snippet

events.direction: Neither for nor against; a reduction between T and T^eq.

events.what_happened: Itay Kaplan and Nicholas Ramsey, 'On Kim-Independence' (arXiv 1702.03894, v1 13 Feb 2017; v2 8 Jan 2019). Defines Kim-independence for NSOP1 theories; shows a Kim's-lemma version, local character, symmetry and the independence theorem, each characterising NSOP1. Published Journal of the European Mathematical Society 22 (2020), 1423-1474 (per search snippet). Mutchnik's talk abstract says a global variant of the simple Kim-forking conjecture follows from this work.
events.delivers: A framework for independence in NSOP1 theories; not a result on the bullet's conjecture. Its relevance is as the background for the NSOP1 variant.
events.remains: Not applicable: a different question (Kim-independence, NSOP1). Discarded for this bullet.
events.direction: Not applicable to the bullet: a different independence notion in a different class.

events.what_happened: Daniel Max Hoffmann and Anand Pillay, 'Thorn forking, weak normality, and theories with selectors' (arXiv 2006.15630, v1 28 Jun 2020; v2 2 Sep 2022). Commentary on Ealy and Onshuus's 'Thorn forking and stable forking'; gives a counterexample to Corollary 4.2 of that paper, concerning strong dividing and dcl(c). Published Journal of Symbolic Logic 88(4) (2023) per search snippet. The authors say that although the commented paper appears to shed light on the stable forking conjecture, there is still no real connection with it.
events.revisions: v1 28 Jun 2020; v2 2 Sep 2022 (substantially modified after referee comments, per the comments field).
events.delivers: A counterexample to a corollary about thorn forking and strong dividing. It is about a different notion (thorn/strong dividing), and by the authors' own account it has no connection to the stable forking conjecture. Discarded for this bullet, with that reason.
events.remains: Not applicable. Discarded for this bullet.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published (2023), per search snippet; the arXiv page lists no journal reference

events.direction: Not applicable to the bullet; counterexample to a thorn-forking corollary.

events.what_happened: John Baldwin, James Freitag and Scott Mutchnik, 'Simple Homogeneous Structures and Indiscernible Sequence Invariants' (arXiv 2405.08211; v1 13 May 2024, v2 2 Oct 2024, v3 28 Apr 2026). Abstract (paraphrased; full text not read): proves variants of the simple Kim-forking conjecture, an NSOP1 analogue of the stable forking conjecture: a global version with infinitely many variables in every NSOP1 theory; a finite-variable version when F_Mb(p) is finite; and a nontrivial instance of the full NSOP1 conjecture in low NSOP1 theories or for isolated types with the definable Morley property. Also resolves a conjecture of Koponen (simple theories with QE in a finite relational language have finite rank and are one-based). Mutchnik gave a seminar talk 'Toward the simple Kim-forking conjecture', joint with Baldwin and Freitag, on 5 Dec 2024 (Indico event 13421); the talk abstract is the same material in summary.
events.revisions: v1 13 May 2024; v2 2 Oct 2024; v3 28 Apr 2026 (current).
events.delivers: Variants and special cases of the NSOP1 simple Kim-forking conjecture (Kim-forking with Kim-independence, global and finite-variable versions, and instances in low or isolated cases). These address the NSOP1 analogue. They are not a result on simple theories under the bullet's formulation as I read it.
events.remains: The bullet's conjecture for simple theories is not touched. The full simple Kim-forking conjecture for general NSOP1 theories remains open per the abstract.
events.direction: Positive partial results for the NSOP1 analogue; no direction on the simple-theory conjecture.

events.what_happened: Alberto Miguel-Gomez, 'On stable Kim-forking and rosy theories' (arXiv 2503.23936, v1 31 Mar 2025, single version). Abstract: answers in part a question of Kim and d'Elbee; assuming the stable Kim-forking conjecture (the NSOP1 variant of the stable forking conjecture), every NSOP1 rosy theory is simple; also proves that the theory of a Frobenius field has stable Kim-forking over algebraically closed sets. The arXiv page lists DOI 10.1017/jsl.2025.10173, a Journal of Symbolic Logic DOI; I did not confirm acceptance or the publication date.
events.delivers: Conditional on the stable Kim-forking conjecture for NSOP1 theories: every NSOP1 rosy theory is simple. Unconditional: the Frobenius field theory has stable Kim-forking. This concerns the NSOP1 variant, a different property from the bullet's formulation. The class of simple theories is inside NSOP1, so the NSOP1 variant can bear on simple theories only if its formulation over models specialises to forking there; I did not verify that from the paper body.
events.remains: The NSOP1 stable Kim-forking conjecture is not proved; whether a non-simple NSOP1 rosy theory exists remains open.

checked_by.who: Journal of Symbolic Logic (refereed journal), per the DOI on the arXiv page
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record in model theory
checked_by.what_they_did: Listed DOI 10.1017/jsl.2025.10173 on the arXiv page; acceptance and refereeing not confirmed

events.direction: Conditional partial answer to an NSOP1 question; positive evidence for the NSOP1 variant on Frobenius fields.

events.what_happened: Scott Mutchnik, 'Topic Seminar: Forking', UIC Logic Seminar, 7 October 2025 (seminar abstract, not a paper). The abstract says that for supersimple countably categorical theories, stability of a global forking relation is equivalent to the stable forking conjecture; it then reports simple Kim-forking results from joint work with Baldwin and Freitag (the same material as arXiv 2405.08211). The 2026 paper arXiv 2607.09069 cites the countably categorical equivalence as a consequence of Corollary 4.4 of Palacin and Wagner rather than as a new result.
events.delivers: A claimed equivalence within a restricted class (supersimple countably categorical theories): global forking stability is equivalent to the stable forking conjecture. The equivalence is a reduction; it does not decide either side.
events.remains: Whether global forking stability holds for supersimple countably categorical theories, and so the conjecture for that class.
events.direction: Reduction within a restricted class; neither for nor against the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Scott Mutchnik, 'Reducing stable forking dependence to finitely many pregeometries' (arXiv 2607.09069; v1 10 Jul 2026, v2 11 Sep 2026, v3 28 Sep 2026; 34 pages). Theorem 1 (per the v3 introduction): for each n there is a finite set G_n of pregeometries such that, for any finite-rank supersimple T, stability of forking over a base for rank-n types is equivalent to no pregeometry in G_n embedding in an SU-rank-1 partial type. The paper calls this the main case of the stable forking conjecture (stability over a base in finite-rank supersimple theories). It says the rank-3 main part was accomplished by Peretz, that the argument does not extend as stated to higher ranks, and turns Peretz's universal result into an existence theorem for n > 3.
events.revisions: v1 10 Jul 2026; v2 11 Sep 2026; v3 28 Sep 2026 (current). I read v3 only through its first 100,000 characters.
events.delivers: A reduction, not a proof of stability: stability of forking over a base in finite-SU-rank supersimple theories is equivalent to a finite check per rank (G_n finite). The paper's own summary is that the case 'is determined by finitely many pregeometries in each rank'. It does not state that stability holds in any new case.
events.remains: Whether forking is stable over a base in finite-SU-rank supersimple theories. The paper says that even under SU-rank 3, the strongest assumptions under which the full conjecture remains open, stability over a base also remains open. Infinite-rank and non-supersimple simple theories are outside the result.
events.direction: Neither for nor against the conjecture; a reduction of one restricted case. Consistent with the 2609.00436 counterexample being of infinite rank (the authors' §1.1 says they searched for an infinite-rank counterexample because finite rank is highly constrained).

events.what_happened: James Freitag and Scott Mutchnik, 'A counterexample to the stable forking conjecture' (arXiv 2609.00436, 21 pages, math.LO/math.QA; one version, v1, 31 Aug 2026 22:17 UTC, as of my check on 13 Oct 2026). Abstract: 'Using ChatGPT 5.6, we find a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture. This answers a long-standing open question of Hart, Kim and Pillay (1996).' Counterexample: T^(not StFk), the theory of an infinite-dimensional module over the division ring of fractions of the quantum graph algebra of the random bipartite graph, with sorts for the graph and the module and the module action indexed by graph vertices (§1.2, §3). §4.1 argues the theory is simple, in fact supersimple, by checking Kim-Pillay axioms for a candidate independence relation defined through spans of module coordinates (Fact 4.1, Claim 4.3, Proposition 4.4). §4.2 shows forking over the empty set is unstable: Lemma 4.5 gives that the spans U_i and W_j intersect trivially exactly when not E(i,j); saturation plus an Erdos-Rado indiscernible sequence of pairs gives the order property; the authors then argue that a stable formula could not witness forking (following Remark 7.5 of Baldwin-Mutchnik and Palacin-Wagner §4). Theorem 1.3 (§1), as I read it through the HTML: 'The stable forking conjecture is false.' The authors also write that it 'seems unlikely that this counterexample would have been found in the near term without the use of generative AI'.
events.revisions: v1 only (31 Aug 2026), per the arXiv abstract page checked on 13 Oct 2026. No later version found.
events.delivers: If the argument holds: a single simple (indeed supersimple) theory of infinite rank in which forking is not witnessed by stable formulas, refuting the universal claim in the form the authors state (their Conjecture 1.2, the Hart-Kim-Pillay formulation). One example refutes a universal claim, and it is itself a simple theory, so it is inside the bullet's scope.
events.remains: Nothing else in the bullet remains refuted or open by this single example: the authors' own text and the Mutchnik 2026 paper leave finite-rank cases and countably categorical simple theories open. Whether the refutation extends to the other formulations of the conjecture is not addressed in what I read.
events.directly_checkable: No single finite object. The claim rests on the proofs in §4 (the Kim-Pillay axioms in §4.1 and the instability lemma and indiscernible argument in §4.2), which a model theorist could check by hand. No Lean, computer or other formal check is reported.
events.doubts: (1) The authors' AI disclosure is inconsistent in the text I read. The title-page footnote says 'the arguments in this paper were based on proofs generated using JF's ChatGPT account'; §1.1 says 'The proofs of the relevant facts around the counterexample as well as some aspects of the specific setup have been written entirely by the authors, and no AI tool was used in the actual writing of this manuscript.' Both can hold only if generated proofs were rewritten by the authors, which the paper does not say. (2) Several verification steps are deferred in the text as I read it (through the HTML summaries): in §4.1 'But this is just as in the proof of base monotonicity' and 'This follows via saturation, but we want a bit more'; local character is 'by similar reasoning to before'; §4.2 has 'by substitutions, one can see that rX_jX_i = rX_iX_j'. Lemma 4.5's statement writes alpha_j where beta_j is meant. The step X_jX_i - X_iX_j = 2X_jX_i != 0 depends on a sign or characteristic condition that I did not find stated in the parts read. These are points for a checker, not confirmed errors. (3) An automated arXiv overview on alphaxiv (not a source) says the paper itself flags a possible reversal of indexing in the final order-pattern argument. I did not find such a flag in the text I read and cannot confirm it either way. (4) No review, journal submission reported, citing paper, or public assessment by a model theorist was found as of 13 Oct 2026. MathWorld (last updated 2 Oct 2026) reports that no independent external verification had been reported as of 7 Sep 2026; the Breakthrough Tracker (last checked 4 Sep 2026) says no independent specialist assessment, formal proof or separate construction had been located. (5) Co-author Mutchnik's revision of arXiv 2607.09069 (v3, 28 Sep 2026) describes the full stable forking conjecture as open for SU-rank 3 and, in the first 100,000 characters I read, does not mention 2609.00436.
events.direction: Against the conjecture as the authors state it: it exhibits a simple theory in which forking is not witnessed by stable formulas, so the universal claim fails. The authors' Theorem 1.3 reads 'The stable forking conjecture is false.'
events.object: T^(not StFk): the theory of an infinite-dimensional module over the division ring of fractions of the quantum graph algebra of the random bipartite graph; sorts for the graph and the module; module action indexed by graph vertices (§1.2, §3). It is shown supersimple (§4.1) and forking over the empty set is shown to be unstable (§4.2), so no stable formula can witness forking as the conjecture requires. The theory itself is explicit; the instability witness uses saturation and an Erdos-Rado indiscernible sequence, so that step is non-constructive.

systems.name: ChatGPT 5.6
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors, it was the system used to find the counterexample: the abstract says 'Using ChatGPT 5.6, we find a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture.' The introduction says the authors 'prompted ChatGPT to construct a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture with a detailed series of prompts which took into account the many restrictions and likely restrictions such a counterexample would have to satisfy', and that it was prompted to use the standard strategy of proving simplicity and characterising forking by an abstract independence relation. The title-page footnote says 'the arguments in this paper were based on proofs generated using JF's ChatGPT account'. Whether 'ChatGPT 5.6' and 'GPT-5.6 Sol' (the name in §1.1) are the same system is not stated in the paper.
systems.basis_quote: Using ChatGPT 5.6, we find a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture.

systems.name: GPT-5.6 Sol
systems.what_it_did: Per §1.1 of the authors' paper, it proved the result with the authors: 'This is an AI-generated result proven with the help of GPT-5.6 Sol.' The same section says the proofs of the relevant facts and some aspects of the setup 'have been written entirely by the authors, and no AI tool was used in the actual writing of this manuscript', and that AI 'was used for proofreading, with the edits performed and evaluated manually by the authors'. The authors also write that 'it seems unlikely that this counterexample would have been found in the near term without the use of generative AI'. Whether GPT-5.6 Sol is a shipped model, an internal build or a Pro configuration is not stated in the paper.
systems.basis_quote: This is an AI-generated result proven with the help of GPT-5.6 Sol.

ai.disclosed_cost: Title-page footnote: 'SM additionally received a grant of access to ChatGPT Pro through OpenAI's academic researcher support program'. This is an access grant. No token, compute or dollar figures found.

disputes.summary: Who produced the proofs. The paper's title-page footnote says 'the arguments in this paper were based on proofs generated using JF's ChatGPT account', while §1.1 says the proofs of the relevant facts 'have been written entirely by the authors'. Secondary accounts go further than the paper: MathWorld says 'GPT-5.6 Sol supplied the counterexample and central arguments during interactive research, and the authors developed and checked the proof'; the Breakthrough Tracker says guided prompts to GPT-5.6 Sol 'produced the counterexample and supporting proof route' while the authors 'wrote and checked the final arguments'. The later pass should weigh the authors' own sentences; I recorded them as written.

Two model names for one credited system. The abstract says 'ChatGPT 5.6'; §1.1 says 'GPT-5.6 Sol'. The paper does not say whether these are one system, and the secondary sources use both strings. Whether either is a shipped model is not established in the paper.

summary: Searched 38 times and read about 30 pages. The event that bears on the bullet is Freitag and Mutchnik's arXiv 2609.00436 (31 Aug 2026, one version as of 13 Oct 2026, 21 pages). It claims 'Using ChatGPT 5.6, we find a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture'. The example is an infinite-rank supersimple (hence simple) theory whose forking relation is unstable, so no stable formula witnesses forking over the empty set. I read the paper through the arXiv HTML using WebFetch, which returns summaries rather than verbatim text; the PDF yielded no readable text, and I did not open the copy the tool saved outside this project directory. From those summaries the §4.1 simplicity argument and the §4.2 instability argument are present and detailed, but several verification steps are deferred to 'similar reasoning' and I did not check the algebra. No independent verification appears in any source I could reach: MathWorld (updated 2 Oct 2026) says none was reported as of 7 Sep; the Breakthrough Tracker (4 Sep) says no specialist assessment, formal proof or separate construction was located; and I found no arXiv comment, citing paper, or mathematician's public assessment after that. Mathstodon and Bluesky could not be searched directly; the only Bluesky item was a social-media post quoted in a news alert, which is not an assessment of the proof. The closest call for the second pass is the AI role. The authors' §1.1 says 'This is an AI-generated result proven with the help of GPT-5.6 Sol' and that the counterexample 'seems unlikely' to have been found without generative AI, yet the title-page footnote says the arguments 'were based on proofs generated using JF's ChatGPT account', and the same section says the proofs were 'written entirely by the authors'. I recorded the authors' own words and the disagreement. Before 2026 the conjecture was open by all sources I found, with partial results recorded above: Kim 2001 (one-based simple theories with EHI); Peretz 2004 (SU-rank 2, supersimple omega-categorical); Pourmahdian 2003 (Fraisse-Hrushovski theories with forking = d-independence); Palacin and Wagner 2010 and Palacin 2011 (CM-trivial and strong stable forking); Casanovas and Potier 2015 (T versus T^eq equivalence). In 2026 Mutchnik's arXiv 2607.09069 reduces the finite-rank supersimple case to finitely many pregeometries per rank; that is a reduction, not a proof, and it says even SU-rank 3 remains open. This is consistent with the counterexample being infinite-rank. The NSOP1 'simple Kim-forking' results (Baldwin, Freitag, Mutchnik 2024; Miguel-Gomez 2025, conditional) are, as I read them, a different question. However, NSOP1 contains the simple theories, so whether the NSOP1 conjecture bears on simple theories depends on its over-models formulation, which I did not verify. The Wikipedia bullet is loose: its Model theory entry reads 'The stable forking conjecture for simple theories' with no formulation given, and sources say the conjecture has several formalisations with counterexamples already known for many (Peretz 2004). I could not identify which earlier counterexample, if any, refutes the formulation the bullet intends. The 1996 date for the conjecture comes from the 2026 abstract's citation of Hart, Kim and Pillay; I did not verify it independently. Hoffmann and Pillay (2020/2023) is recorded and discarded because it concerns thorn forking, and its authors say it has no real connection to the conjecture.
competing_reading: Against treating 2609.00436 as settling the bullet: the bullet names no formulation, and the authors refute the Hart-Kim-Pillay formulation as they state it (their Conjecture 1.2). If the bullet means a different formulation, the example may refute a neighbour rather than the bullet, and earlier sources say counterexamples to some formulations were already known. Also, nothing independent has checked a 21-page, unrefereed argument with deferred steps, and the instability argument could fail at Lemma 4.5 or at the indiscernible-sequence step. For reading it as settling it: the example is a simple theory, the authors state the conjecture is false, and the standard form cited across the sources ('every simple theory has stable forking') is the one it refutes. On the AI question, the strongest reading against the model's contribution being load-bearing is the authors' 'no AI tool was used in the actual writing' sentence; the strongest reading for it is the §1.1 'AI-generated result' sentence, the 'unlikely ... without the use of generative AI' sentence, and the footnote about proofs generated using a ChatGPT account.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A referee report, journal acceptance, or a written expert check of §4.1 (Kim-Pillay axioms) and §4.2 (Lemma 4.5 and the indiscernible-sequence argument), including the characteristic condition behind the sign step. (2) An explicit statement from the authors reconciling the 'proofs generated using JF's ChatGPT account' footnote with the §1.1 'written entirely by the authors' sentence, and saying which system and version (ChatGPT 5.6 or GPT-5.6 Sol) produced which steps. (3) Confirmation from the paper body, not an overview, of whether it flags an index reversal in the final order-pattern argument. (4) Identifying which formulation the Wikipedia bullet means, and checking the refuted formulation against it, including whether Kim-Pillay 2001's strong-version claim is actually in that paper. (5) Any later version of arXiv 2609.00436 or citing work that engages with the proof.

event.what_happened: James Freitag and Scott Mutchnik, 'A counterexample to the stable forking conjecture' (arXiv 2609.00436, 21 pages, math.LO/math.QA; one version, v1, 31 Aug 2026 22:17 UTC, as of my check on 13 Oct 2026). Abstract: 'Using ChatGPT 5.6, we find a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture. This answers a long-standing open question of Hart, Kim and Pillay (1996).' Counterexample: T^(not StFk), the theory of an infinite-dimensional module over the division ring of fractions of the quantum graph algebra of the random bipartite graph, with sorts for the graph and the module and the module action indexed by graph vertices (§1.2, §3). §4.1 argues the theory is simple, in fact supersimple, by checking Kim-Pillay axioms for a candidate independence relation defined through spans of module coordinates (Fact 4.1, Claim 4.3, Proposition 4.4). §4.2 shows forking over the empty set is unstable: Lemma 4.5 gives that the spans U_i and W_j intersect trivially exactly when not E(i,j); saturation plus an Erdos-Rado indiscernible sequence of pairs gives the order property; the authors then argue that a stable formula could not witness forking (following Remark 7.5 of Baldwin-Mutchnik and Palacin-Wagner §4). Theorem 1.3 (§1), as I read it through the HTML: 'The stable forking conjecture is false.' The authors also write that it 'seems unlikely that this counterexample would have been found in the near term without the use of generative AI'.
event.revisions: v1 only (31 Aug 2026), per the arXiv abstract page checked on 13 Oct 2026. No later version found.
event.delivers: If the argument holds: a single simple (indeed supersimple) theory of infinite rank in which forking is not witnessed by stable formulas, refuting the universal claim in the form the authors state (their Conjecture 1.2, the Hart-Kim-Pillay formulation). One example refutes a universal claim, and it is itself a simple theory, so it is inside the bullet's scope.
event.remains: Nothing else in the bullet remains refuted or open by this single example: the authors' own text and the Mutchnik 2026 paper leave finite-rank cases and countably categorical simple theories open. Whether the refutation extends to the other formulations of the conjecture is not addressed in what I read.
event.directly_checkable: No single finite object. The claim rests on the proofs in §4 (the Kim-Pillay axioms in §4.1 and the instability lemma and indiscernible argument in §4.2), which a model theorist could check by hand. No Lean, computer or other formal check is reported.
event.doubts: (1) The authors' AI disclosure is inconsistent in the text I read. The title-page footnote says 'the arguments in this paper were based on proofs generated using JF's ChatGPT account'; §1.1 says 'The proofs of the relevant facts around the counterexample as well as some aspects of the specific setup have been written entirely by the authors, and no AI tool was used in the actual writing of this manuscript.' Both can hold only if generated proofs were rewritten by the authors, which the paper does not say. (2) Several verification steps are deferred in the text as I read it (through the HTML summaries): in §4.1 'But this is just as in the proof of base monotonicity' and 'This follows via saturation, but we want a bit more'; local character is 'by similar reasoning to before'; §4.2 has 'by substitutions, one can see that rX_jX_i = rX_iX_j'. Lemma 4.5's statement writes alpha_j where beta_j is meant. The step X_jX_i - X_iX_j = 2X_jX_i != 0 depends on a sign or characteristic condition that I did not find stated in the parts read. These are points for a checker, not confirmed errors. (3) An automated arXiv overview on alphaxiv (not a source) says the paper itself flags a possible reversal of indexing in the final order-pattern argument. I did not find such a flag in the text I read and cannot confirm it either way. (4) No review, journal submission reported, citing paper, or public assessment by a model theorist was found as of 13 Oct 2026. MathWorld (last updated 2 Oct 2026) reports that no independent external verification had been reported as of 7 Sep 2026; the Breakthrough Tracker (last checked 4 Sep 2026) says no independent specialist assessment, formal proof or separate construction had been located. (5) Co-author Mutchnik's revision of arXiv 2607.09069 (v3, 28 Sep 2026) describes the full stable forking conjecture as open for SU-rank 3 and, in the first 100,000 characters I read, does not mention 2609.00436.
event.direction: Against the conjecture as the authors state it: it exhibits a simple theory in which forking is not witnessed by stable formulas, so the universal claim fails. The authors' Theorem 1.3 reads 'The stable forking conjecture is false.'
event.object: T^(not StFk): the theory of an infinite-dimensional module over the division ring of fractions of the quantum graph algebra of the random bipartite graph; sorts for the graph and the module; module action indexed by graph vertices (§1.2, §3). It is shown supersimple (§4.1) and forking over the empty set is shown to be unstable (§4.2), so no stable formula can witness forking as the conjecture requires. The theory itself is explicit; the instability witness uses saturation and an Erdos-Rado indiscernible sequence, so that step is non-constructive.

systems.name: ChatGPT 5.6
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors, it was the system used to find the counterexample: the abstract says 'Using ChatGPT 5.6, we find a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture.' The introduction says the authors 'prompted ChatGPT to construct a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture with a detailed series of prompts which took into account the many restrictions and likely restrictions such a counterexample would have to satisfy', and that it was prompted to use the standard strategy of proving simplicity and characterising forking by an abstract independence relation. The title-page footnote says 'the arguments in this paper were based on proofs generated using JF's ChatGPT account'. Whether 'ChatGPT 5.6' and 'GPT-5.6 Sol' (the name in §1.1) are the same system is not stated in the paper.

judgement.why: The statement is a single universal claim about all simple theories, so one simple theory in which forking is not witnessed by stable formulas refutes the whole of it: the Freitag-Mutchnik event is scope whole, direction refuted, object a counterexample. It is a 43-day-old preprint and nobody has engaged with it, so it is unreviewed. The theory itself is explicit, but checking it means working through proofs, not a simple direct check, so it is not checkable. I kept it credible: the authors are established in the field, the argument is detailed, and the doubts the record lists (steps deferred to 'similar reasoning', a typo, an unstated sign condition) are points for a checker, not identified errors. Mutchnik's Sept 2026 paper calling the conjecture open in SU-rank 3 fits an infinite-rank counterexample. AI role is generated: the abstract says the counterexample was found 'using ChatGPT 5.6', and §1.1 calls it 'an AI-generated result'. The sentence that the authors wrote the manuscript themselves concerns the writing, which does not take away from the AI producing the construction. The pre-2024 restricted-class results are cases, digested by journal publication. Kim-Pillay, Casanovas-Potier, Hoffmann-Pillay, the seminar and the 2026 pregeometry paper are reductions or not about this question, so none. The NSOP1 and strong-version results are variants.
judgement.doubts: The statement names no formulation. The counterexample refutes the Hart-Kim-Pillay formulation, which the record takes as the standard one. If the list meant some other formulation, scope could be a neighbouring variant instead. Palacin-Wagner's link to stable forking comes only through Mutchnik's 2026 citation. The AI disclosure is internally inconsistent: the footnote says the proofs were generated, while §1.1 says they were written by the authors.
